title: UNIT 5: CHEMICAL BONDING
notes:
✓ Chemical bonding → The attraction that holds atoms or ions together.

Atoms form bonds to reach a more stable, lower-energy electron arrangement, often similar to that of a noble gas.

title: 5.1 Why Atoms Form Chemical Bonds
notes:
✓ Atoms form chemical bonds because bonded atoms usually have lower potential energy and greater stability than separated atoms.

Atoms achieve stability mainly by gaining, losing or sharing valence electrons.

title: 5.1.1 Ion and Formation of Ions
notes:
✓ Ion → An atom or group of atoms with a net electrical charge caused by gaining or losing electrons.

✓ Cation → Positive ion formed by losing electrons.
Example: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻.

✓ Anion → Negative ion formed by gaining electrons.
Example: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.

title: 5.2 Ionic Bonding
notes:
✓ Ionic bonding → The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

It usually forms when a metal transfers one or more electrons to a non-metal.

◆ EXAMPLE
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl.

title: 5.2.1 Formation of an Ionic Bond
notes:
✓ An ionic bond forms through electron transfer followed by electrostatic attraction.

◆ EXAMPLE: NaCl
• Sodium loses one valence electron → Na⁺.
• Chlorine gains one electron → Cl⁻.
• Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract each other to form an ionic lattice.

✓ The overall compound is electrically neutral.

title: 5.2.2 Lewis Formulas of Ionic Compounds
notes:
✓ Lewis electron-dot formulas → Show valence electrons and the formation of ions.

◆ EXAMPLE
NaCl → [Na]⁺ [:Cl:]⁻

The chloride ion is shown with a complete octet, while sodium is shown as Na⁺ after losing its valence electron.

◆ OTHER EXAMPLES
• MgCl₂ → Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻.
• CaO → Ca²⁺ + O²⁻.

title: 5.2.3 Examples of Ionic Compounds
notes:
◆ Common ionic compounds:
• NaCl → sodium chloride.
• MgO → magnesium oxide.
• CaCl₂ → calcium chloride.
• KBr → potassium bromide.
• Al₂O₃ → aluminium oxide.

✓ They contain cations and anions arranged in a crystal lattice.

title: 5.2.4 General Properties of Ionic Compounds
notes:
◆ Ionic compounds generally:
• Have high melting and boiling points.
• Are hard and brittle crystalline solids.
• Often dissolve in water.
• Do not conduct electricity as solids because ions are fixed.
• Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved because ions are mobile.
• Have strong electrostatic attractions between ions.

title: 5.3 Covalent Bonding
notes:
✓ Covalent bonding → Occurs when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

It usually occurs between non-metal atoms.

◆ EXAMPLE
H + H → H–H

Each hydrogen shares one electron and obtains a stable two-electron arrangement.

title: 5.3.1 Lewis Formulas of Covalent Molecules
notes:
✓ Lewis structures → Show valence electrons, shared electron pairs and lone pairs.

◆ EXAMPLES
H₂ → H–H → single bond.
O₂ → O=O → double bond.
N₂ → N≡N → triple bond.
H₂O → H–O–H with two lone pairs on oxygen.

✓ A line represents one shared electron pair.

title: 5.3.2 Types of Covalent Bonds
notes:
✓ Single bond → One shared electron pair.
Example: H–H.

✓ Double bond → Two shared electron pairs.
Example: O=O.

✓ Triple bond → Three shared electron pairs.
Example: N≡N.

✓ Multiple bonds are generally stronger and shorter than single bonds between the same atoms.

title: 5.3.3 Examples of Covalent Molecules
notes:
◆ Simple covalent molecules include:
• H₂ → hydrogen.
• Cl₂ → chlorine.
• H₂O → water.
• NH₃ → ammonia.
• CH₄ → methane.
• CO₂ → carbon dioxide.

Covalent molecules may contain single, double or triple bonds.

title: 5.3.4 Polarity in Covalent Molecules
notes:
✓ Polarity → Results from unequal sharing of electrons between atoms with different electronegativities.

✓ Polar molecule → Has an uneven distribution of charge and a net dipole.

✓ Nonpolar molecule → Has no net dipole because charge is distributed evenly or bond dipoles cancel.

title: 5.3.5 Polar vs Nonpolar Covalent Molecules
notes:
◆ POLAR
• Unequal charge distribution.
• Has a net dipole.
• Examples → H₂O and NH₃.

◆ NONPOLAR
• No net dipole.
• Symmetrical molecules can have bond dipoles that cancel.
• Examples → H₂, Cl₂ and CO₂.

✓ IMPORTANT
A molecule can contain polar bonds but still be nonpolar if its geometry causes the bond dipoles to cancel.

title: 5.4 Coordinate Covalent (Dative) Bond
notes:
✓ Coordinate covalent bond → A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair are supplied by one atom.

◆ EXAMPLE
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺

Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form the new N–H bond.

✓ After formation, the coordinate bond behaves like an ordinary covalent bond.

title: 5.4.1 Conditions for Coordinate Bond Formation
notes:
✓ Coordinate covalent bonding requires:
• A donor atom with a lone pair of electrons.
• An acceptor atom or ion with an available orbital or electron deficiency.

◆ EXAMPLES
• NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺.
• H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺.

title: 5.5 General Properties of Covalent Compounds
notes:
◆ Molecular covalent compounds generally:
• Have relatively low melting and boiling points.
• Exist as gases, liquids or soft solids.
• Usually do not conduct electricity.
• Often have poor solubility in water.
• May dissolve in nonpolar organic solvents.

✓ Exception → Giant covalent structures such as diamond and silicon dioxide have very high melting points.

title: 5.5.1 Melting and Boiling of Covalent Compounds
notes:
✓ Simple molecular covalent substances usually have low melting and boiling points because the intermolecular forces between molecules are relatively weak compared with ionic or giant covalent bonding.

✓ Stronger intermolecular forces generally increase melting and boiling points.

title: 5.5.2 Electrical Conductivity of Covalent Compounds
notes:
✓ Most simple covalent compounds do not conduct electricity because they do not contain freely moving charged particles.

✓ Exceptions exist when covalent substances ionize in solution, such as acids that produce ions in water.

title: 5.6 Metallic Bonding
notes:
✓ Metallic bonding → The attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized valence electrons throughout a metal lattice.

The electrons are not attached to one particular atom and can move through the structure.

title: 5.6.1 Electrical Conductivity of Metals
notes:
✓ Metals conduct electricity because their delocalized electrons can move through the metal when an electric field is applied.

The mobile electrons carry electrical charge without requiring the metal atoms themselves to move.

title: 5.6.2 Thermal Conductivity of Metals
notes:
✓ Metals conduct heat efficiently because mobile electrons transfer energy rapidly through the metal lattice.

The closely packed metal particles also help transfer vibrational energy.

title: 5.6.3 Other Properties of Metallic Bonding
notes:
◆ Metallic bonding explains why metals are generally:
• Malleable → Can be hammered into sheets.
• Ductile → Can be drawn into wires.
• Lustrous → Reflect light.
• Strong and durable.

Metal ions can shift positions while remaining attracted to the delocalized electrons, allowing metals to deform without the structure immediately breaking.

title: UNIT 5 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ Chemical bonding → Attraction that holds atoms or ions together.
✓ Atoms bond → To achieve greater stability and lower energy.

◆ IONIC
• Electron transfer.
• Metal + non-metal.
• Cation + anion.
• Strong electrostatic attraction.
• High melting/boiling points.
• Conducts when molten or aqueous.

◆ COVALENT
• Electron sharing.
• Usually non-metal + non-metal.
• Single, double or triple bonds.
• Usually low melting/boiling points for simple molecules.
• Usually poor electrical conductors.

◆ POLARITY
Polar → Unequal charge distribution + net dipole.
Nonpolar → No net dipole.

◆ COORDINATE COVALENT
Both bonding electrons come from one atom.

◆ METALLIC
Positive metal ions + delocalized electrons.
Good electrical and thermal conductivity.
Malleable and ductile.

✓ EXAM TIP
Ionic = transfer.
Covalent = sharing.
Coordinate = one atom supplies both shared electrons.
Metallic = delocalized electrons.
